issues.item: Triggers: Power Imbalance: Being in a situation where someone has power over me
issues.explanation: The trigger 'being in a situation where someone has power over me' is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type of natural disaster and with the rest of the profile, which otherwise emphasizes alarm/reactivity and fragmented recall rather than interpersonal domination or coercion. For this trauma type, this item introduces an implausible trigger theme not supported elsewhere in threat, memory, or appraisals.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: Avoiding hospitals/ambulances/physical examinations is not well supported by the rest of the profile for a natural-disaster trauma. There are no memory or threat items involving injury treatment, medical rescue, or bodily harm, so this strategy appears to target a symptom theme not represented elsewhere. In contrast, the profile is centered on generalized alarm, shouting, unpredictability, and fragmented memory.

issues.item: Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
issues.explanation: Self-harm is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile and trauma context: the other selected items describe a classic hyperarousal/re-experiencing natural-disaster PTSD presentation with avoidance and overeating, but no accompanying items suggest the kind of shame, self-punitive appraisal, dissociative affect regulation, or broader emotion-dysregulation pattern that would make physical self-harm clinically coherent here. It stands out as addressing a symptom process not otherwise represented in the five components.

Alcohol smell is not impossible, but in this profile it is weakly anchored to the reported trauma type and the rest of the item set. The other triggers (unpredictability, shouting) fit a danger/hyperarousal formulation, whereas alcohol smell implies a very specific sensory trauma cue that is not supported by the memory or threat items. Given a natural-disaster index trauma, this trigger is difficult to explain clinically without additional corroborating content.

vignette: Kofi had always been drawn to high-stress jobs, but nothing could have prepared him for the day a massive earthquake struck his hometown. As a bomb disposal technician, he was part of the emergency response team that rushed to the scene. The sounds of crumbling buildings and screams still echoed in his mind - loud noises that now made him jump at any moment. Shouting, too, transported him back to those chaotic hours, when every second counted and lives hung in the balance. Unpredictable situations, which had once been a thrilling aspect of his work, now filled him with dread. In the months following the disaster, Kofi found himself struggling to cope with these triggers. He began to eat excessively, using food as a distraction from the anxiety that gripped him. Avoiding anything stressful became second nature - he would turn down invitations to social events or decline tasks at work if they seemed too taxing. Keeping his mind occupied all the time was another tactic; he'd spend hours watching TV or scrolling through his phone to prevent any quiet moments where memories might creep in. But despite these efforts, Kofi's body continued to react as if it were still in danger. False alarms went off constantly - a sudden noise would make him leap out of bed, ready to respond to an emergency that wasn't there. Flashbacks hit without warning, and he'd find himself reliving the earthquake, his heart racing as if it were happening all over again. When these episodes passed, Kofi was left shaken, wondering why his mind couldn't shake off the feeling of being constantly on edge. The memories themselves remained fragmented - Kofi would push them away before they became too vivid, afraid of what he might recall. But when he did remember snippets, intense rage would flood through him. It made no sense to his rational mind, but the emotions lingered long after the memories faded. These incomplete recollections haunted him, leaving more questions than answers. As time passed, Kofi's maladaptive strategies only intensified the cycle of threat and memory. Eating excessively led to guilt and self-doubt, which in turn made him more prone to false alarms and flashbacks. Avoiding stressors meant missing out on essential tasks at work, further eroding his sense of control. Keeping his mind occupied all the time left no space for reflection or processing - memories continued to simmer just below the surface, waiting to boil over. Kofi's wife noticed the changes in him, but he pushed her away whenever she tried to talk about it. He was certain that he could handle this on his own, that seeking help would mean admitting weakness. Yet as the months turned into years, Kofi realized he couldn't keep living like this - constantly on edge, trapped in a cycle of fear and avoidance. It was then that he finally sought out professional help, hoping to break free from the hold of those haunting memories and find some semblance of peace. What brought him to therapy was the realization that his work as a bomb disposal technician had become unsustainable - every mission now felt like a threat to his own life. He couldn't shake the feeling that he was one wrong move away from disaster, that his body would always react before his mind could catch up. As Kofi sat in the therapist's office, he knew it wouldn't be easy to confront these demons, but he was ready to try - for himself, and for those around him who deserved a husband, father, and friend who wasn't constantly haunted by the ghosts of that fateful day.
